questions.question: Who were the Kora and the Griqua?
questions.expected_answer: Kora (Korana): Khoikhoi groups who moved north from the south-western Cape in the 18th century as colonists took their land; lived along the middle Orange and lower Vaal rivers in independent clans (e.g. Taaibosch, Links); herders in reed-mat huts; many acquired horses and guns; hunted, traded and raided; spoke !Ora. Griqua: community of mixed Khoikhoi, European, enslaved and other descent denied equal rights in the colony (formerly called Basters); Dutch-speaking Christians with wagons, horses and guns; led by Adam Kok I, Cornelius Kok, Adam Kok II, Barend Barends, Andries Waterboer; settled at Klaarwater (1804), renamed Griquatown (1813); Philippolis (1826).

questions.question: Describe the trade between the Kora and Griqua and the Cape Colony.
questions.expected_answer: From the Cape: manufactured goods - guns, gunpowder and lead, iron tools and pots, cloth and clothing, glass beads, buttons, copper and brass wire; tobacco (used as currency); horses, wagons, pack oxen, saddles. To the Cape: ivory, cattle and sheep, skins and hides, ostrich feathers, karosses. Routes south across the Karoo to Graaff-Reinet, Colesberg, Cape Town. They also traded north and east with the Tswana, acting as middlemen; the colony tried to control the gun trade but smuggling was common.

questions.question: What were the effects of the northern frontier trade?
questions.expected_answer: Wealth and military power for the Kora and Griqua; Griqua captaincies with laws, councils and coins; missions such as Griquatown became trading centres; 1823 Battle of Dithakong - Griqua horsemen with guns (called in by Moffat) defeated attackers; raiding of neighbours for cattle and captives; spread of guns and horses changed warfare and hunting; elephant numbers reduced; later loss of Griqua land (Griqualand West annexed 1871 after diamonds; Adam Kok III's trek to Griqualand East 1861-63).
